20261121-physics-e5-2.material: A car passed through a highway section-speed-enforcement zone (total distance 30 km) in 15 minutes. What is this car's average speed in km per hour?
20261121-physics-e5-2.thinking.0: A car passed through a highway
20261121-physics-e5-2.s.s1.prompt: A car passed through a highway section-speed-enforcement zone (total distance 30 km) in 15 minutes. What is this car's average speed in km per hour?
20261121-physics-e5-2.s.s1.explain: $15$ minutes is $\frac{15}{60} = 0.25$ hours ($\frac{1}{4}$ hour). The average speed is $30\text{ km} \div 0.25\text{ h} = 120\text{ km/h}$.

20261122-physics-e5-1.title: Advanced Data Interpretation
20261122-physics-e5-1.goal: Apply principles of Advanced Data Interpretation to solve the reasoning problem.
20261122-physics-e5-1.material: [Advanced Data Interpretation] On a distance-versus-time graph, which option correctly pairs the physical quantity that the 'slope' of the graph line represents with the state of motion of an object when the slope is a constant straight line?
20261122-physics-e5-1.s.s1.prompt: [Advanced Data Interpretation] On a distance-versus-time graph, which option correctly pairs the physical quantity that the 'slope' of the graph line represents with the state of motion of an object when the slope is a constant straight line?
20261122-physics-e5-1.s.s1.explain: The slope of a time-distance graph is (distance traveled ÷ time), so it represents 'speed', and a straight line with constant slope means 'uniform motion' with constant speed.
20261122-physics-e5-1.s.s1.hint.0: On a graph, (change on the vertical axis ÷ change on the horizontal axis) = (distance ÷ time).

20261122-physics-e5-1.s.s1.o.o3: Time — motion in which direction changes

20261122-physics-e5-2.title: Over the same 60 km distance
20261122-physics-e5-2.goal: Apply principles of Over the same 60 km distance to solve the reasoning problem.
20261122-physics-e5-2.material: Over the same 60 km distance, what is the difference in time taken between a car traveling at 60 km/h and a bus traveling at 30 km/h?
20261122-physics-e5-2.s.s1.prompt: Over the same 60 km distance, what is the difference in time taken between a car traveling at 60 km/h and a bus traveling at 30 km/h?
20261122-physics-e5-2.s.s1.explain: The car takes $60\text{ km} \div 60\text{ km/h} = 1$ hour, and the bus takes $60\text{ km} \div 30\text{ km/h} = 2$ hours, so the bus takes $1$ hour longer.
20261122-physics-e5-2.s.s1.hint.0: Use the formula time = distance ÷ speed.
20261122-physics-e5-2.s.s1.o.o0: The bus takes 1 hour longer than the car

20261122-physics-e5-2.s.s1.o.o2: The two vehicles take exactly the same time
20261122-physics-e5-2.s.s1.o.o3: The bus takes 30 minutes longer than the car

20261122-physics-e6-1.title: Advanced Application
20261122-physics-e6-1.goal: Apply principles of Advanced Application to solve the reasoning problem.
20261122-physics-e6-1.material: [Advanced Application] If you hold a magnifying glass (convex lens) very close to newspaper text, the letters look large and upright, but if you hold it far away, the letters look flipped upside down. Why do the letters look upright when it is held close?
20261122-physics-e6-1.s.s1.prompt: [Advanced Application] If you hold a magnifying glass (convex lens) very close to newspaper text, the letters look large and upright, but if you hold it far away, the letters look flipped upside down. Why do the letters look upright when it is held close?
20261122-physics-e6-1.s.s1.explain: When an object is inside the focal length of a convex lens, the extensions of the refracted light meet and form a virtual image that is larger than the object and upright (an enlarged upright virtual image).
20261122-physics-e6-1.s.s1.hint.0: Think about the path of light when an object is closer than the focal length.
20261122-physics-e6-1.s.s1.hint.1: Since the light spreads out, you have to extend lines backward behind the lens to make them meet.
20261122-physics-e6-1.s.s1.o.o0: Because the text is inside the lens's focal length, and an enlarged upright virtual image is seen
20261122-physics-e6-1.s.s1.o.o1: Because light was regularly reflected like a mirror on the lens surface
20261122-physics-e6-1.s.s1.o.o2: Because the retina of the eye is temporarily enlarged
20261122-physics-e6-1.s.s1.o.o3: Because water vapor in the air heated the magnifying lens

20261122-physics-e6-2.material: What is the scientific reason you must never touch an electric plug or an appliance's switch with wet hands?
20261122-physics-e6-2.thinking.0: What is the scientific reason you must
20261122-physics-e6-2.s.s1.prompt: What is the scientific reason you must never touch an electric plug or an appliance's switch with wet hands?
20261122-physics-e6-2.s.s1.explain: When the skin gets wet, the body's electrical resistance drops sharply to a few tens of times less than usual, and even a low voltage can send a deadly current through the body, causing electric shock accidents.
20261122-physics-e6-2.s.s1.hint.0: Unlike pure water, everyday water contains dissolved electrolytes.
20261122-physics-e6-2.s.s1.hint.1: With wet hands, skin resistance drops sharply and current flows easily.
20261122-physics-e6-2.s.s1.o.o0: Because ions of minerals dissolved in water let electricity pass easily, greatly increasing the risk of electric shock
20261122-physics-e6-2.s.s1.o.o1: Because water droplets cool the plug and make it freeze
20261122-physics-e6-2.s.s1.o.o2: Because magnetic force is generated in wet hands
20261122-physics-e6-2.s.s1.o.o3: Because electricity evaporates all the water on the hands
